lesson_title: Sun, Wind, Water and the Atom
hook_text: Africa has only one nuclear power station, and it is right outside Cape Town.
clip_script: Coal is not the only way to make electricity. In the Northern Cape, fields of solar panels turn sunlight straight into electricity, with no moving parts. Along the Cape coast, wind turbines turn the kinetic energy of moving air into electrical energy. On the Orange River, water rushes from dams through turbines. These sources are renewable: they keep coming back. Then there is Koeberg, Africa's only nuclear power station. It splits uranium atoms in a controlled chain reaction. The heat boils water, steam spins turbines, and generators make electricity, with no carbon dioxide while it runs. The price? Radioactive waste. Low-level waste is buried at Vaalputs in the Northern Cape, and used fuel cools in deep pools at Koeberg. Every energy source has a trade-off. Which would you choose?
visual_style: Aerial solar farm; wind turbines on a coastal ridge; water rushing through a dam wall; an animated uranium nucleus splitting; a blue spent-fuel pool.
pacing: Surprising open, a quick tour of sources, a slower nuclear segment, a question to close.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson and list one advantage and one disadvantage of each source.
